node.label: Kathleen Wilson
node.description: A historian of Britain and its eighteenth-century empire. In her introduction to A New Imperial History, Wilson argues that imperial encounters helped constitute identities within Britain as well as overseas. Difference is an instrument of power, while identities are historically imposed and negotiated through legal status, gender, slavery and performance. She uses Chakrabarty’s challenge to Europe as history’s universal subject and Catherine Hall’s insistence on theorizing difference, without proposing that cultural analysis replace political or social history. Her account of colonial governmentality draws explicitly on Foucault. The later Strolling Players of Empire continues the inquiry through performance and colonial rule. Her work therefore connects cultural and political explanation; it does not treat every imperial setting as identical or empire as a one-way export from a metropolitan centre.
